content: Fungal keratitis is an infection of the cornea caused by fungi. It is more prevalent in low-income countries, particularly in agricultural regions, and is relatively rare in high-income countries. Although antifungal medications are available, their effectiveness remains uncertain. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various antifungal drugs in managing fungal keratitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and clinical trial registries, was conducted. The search included studies up to March 16, 2015, without restrictions on language or publication date. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) focusing on medical treatments for fungal keratitis were included in the analysis. Two reviewers independently selected studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcome of interest was clinical cure (healing of the corneal ulcer) within two to three months. Secondary outcomes included best-corrected visual acuity, time to clinical cure, treatment compliance, adverse effects, and quality of life. A total of 12 trials were included in the review. Of these, 10 were conducted in India, one in Bangladesh, and one in Egypt. Seven trials were deemed to have a high risk of bias in at least one domain, while two trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias across all domains. The studies compared various antifungal treatments, including: 1. Topical 5% natamycin versus topical 1% voriconazole. 2. Topical 5% natamycin versus topical 2% econazole. 3. Topical 5% natamycin versus topical chlorhexidine gluconate (0.05%, 0.1%, and 0.2%). 4. Topical 1% voriconazole versus intrastromal voriconazole (50 µg/0.1 mL), both combined with topical 5% natamycin. 5. Topical 1% voriconazole combined with oral voriconazole versus oral voriconazole and oral itraconazole, both combined with topical 5% natamycin. 6. Topical 1% itraconazole versus topical 1% itraconazole combined with oral itraconazole. 7. Topical amphotericin B versus topical amphotericin B combined with subconjunctival fluconazole injection. 8. Intracameral amphotericin B injection with conventional treatment versus conventional treatment alone for severe fungal ulcers. 9. Topical 0.5% and 1% silver sulphadiazine versus topical 1% miconazole. The results of the review were largely inconclusive due to the limited number of trials available for most comparisons. However, three trials compared topical natamycin with topical voriconazole. In one trial, all 15 participants treated with natamycin achieved clinical cure, compared to 14 out of 15 participants treated with voriconazole (risk ratio [RR] 1.07; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 1.28, low-quality evidence). Another trial reported that participants treated with natamycin were more likely to achieve microbiological cure at six days (RR 1.64; 95% CI 1.38 to 1.94, 299 participants). On average, participants treated with natamycin had better spectacle-corrected visual acuity at two to three months compared to those treated with voriconazole, but the estimate was uncertain (mean difference -0.12 logMAR; 95% CI -0.31 to 0.06, 434 participants; 3 studies, low-quality evidence). Additionally, natamycin was associated with a reduced risk of corneal perforation or the need for therapeutic penetrating keratoplasty (RR 0.61; 95% CI 0.40 to 0.94, 434 participants, high-quality evidence). Evidence on the time to clinical cure was inconclusive. Treatment compliance and quality of life were not reported in the included studies. One trial suggested that natamycin may be more effective than voriconazole in treating fungal keratitis caused by Fusarium species. However, this subgroup analysis was not pre-specified in the review. In conclusion, the included trials were of variable quality and generally underpowered. There is evidence suggesting that natamycin is more effective than voriconazole for treating fungal corneal ulcers. Future research should focus on evaluating treatment efficacy based on the specific fungal species involved.
